full_title: 4.4 Quiz: Sketching with Slope m and y-Intercept b

questions.prompt: To sketch \(y = 4 - \dfrac{2}{3}x\) using \(m\) and \(b\), where do you plot the first point and how do you step to the next point?

choices.text: Plot \((0, 4)\), then move down \(2\) and right \(3\) to \((3, 2)\).
choices.feedback: Rewrite in slope-intercept form as \(y = -\dfrac{2}{3}x + 4\): the \(y\)-intercept is \(b = 4\) at \((0, 4)\), and the slope \(m = -\dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{-2}{3}\) steps down \(2\), right \(3\) to \((3, 2)\).

choices.text: Plot \((0, 4)\), then move up \(2\) and right \(3\) to \((3, 6)\).
choices.feedback: Watch the minus sign in front of \(\dfrac{2}{3}x\)! Rewriting gives \(y = -\dfrac{2}{3}x + 4\), so the slope is negative (down \(2\), right \(3\)), not positive.

choices.text: Plot \(\left(0, -\dfrac{2}{3}\right)\), then move up \(4\) and right \(1\) to \(\left(1, 3\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\).
choices.feedback: Reversed-order trap! The slope \(m\) is ALWAYS the coefficient of \(x\) (\(-\dfrac{2}{3}\)), and the standalone constant \(4\) is the \(y\)-intercept \(b\).

choices.text: Plot \((0, 4)\), then move down \(3\) and right \(2\) to \((2, 1)\).
choices.feedback: Careful — rise is the numerator (\(-2\)) and run is the denominator (\(3\)), not the reverse! Move down \(2\) and right \(3\) to \((3, 2)\).

questions.prompt: Look at the graphed line, its \(y\)-intercept \((0, 2)\), and its dashed rise-and-run triangle below. What is the equation of this line in slope-intercept form?

choices.feedback: You flipped rise and run! Slope is \(\dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{-3}{+5} = -\dfrac{3}{5}\), not \(-\dfrac{5}{3}\).
The \(y\)-intercept is \(b = 2\) at \((0, 2)\), and the dashed triangle shows \(m = \dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{-3}{+5} = -\dfrac{3}{5}\), giving \(y = -\dfrac{3}{5}x + 2\)!
Watch the sign of the slope! The line goes downward from left to right (rise \(= -3\)), so \(m = -\dfrac{3}{5}\), not \(+\dfrac{3}{5}\).
Swapped \(m\) and \(b\)! The slope \(m = -\dfrac{3}{5}\) multiplies \(x\), and the \(y\)-intercept \(b = 2\) is the constant term.

questions.prompt: You are graphing \(y = -\dfrac{3}{4}x - 4\) on a \([-6, 6]\) grid. Starting at \((0, -4)\), going right \(4\) and down \(3\) lands at \((4, -7)\), which falls off the grid! If you reverse both directions (up \(3\) and left \(4\)), what point on the line do you land on?

choices.feedback: You reversed left/right, but you must reverse BOTH directions so the slope stays negative: \(\dfrac{-3}{4} = \dfrac{+3}{-4}\). Moving up \(3\) and left \(4\) from \((0, -4)\) gives \((-4, -1)\).
Careful! Moving up \(3\) and right \(4\) gives a positive slope (\(+\dfrac{3}{4}\)). To keep \(m = -\dfrac{3}{4}\), move up \(3\) and left \(4\) to \((-4, -1)\).
Because \(\dfrac{-3}{4} = \dfrac{+3}{-4}\), moving up \(3\) and left \(4\) from \((0, -4)\) lands at \((0 - 4,\; -4 + 3) = (-4, -1)\) — safely inside the grid and right on the line!
Watch rise vs. run! The vertical move (rise) is \(+3\) (giving \(y = -4 + 3 = -1\)) and the horizontal move (run) is \(-4\) (giving \(x = 0 - 4 = -4\)), so the point is \((-4, -1)\).

questions.prompt: Which equation matches the line graphed below?

choices.feedback: You flipped rise and run! Going from \((0, -2)\) to \((2, 1)\) moves up \(3\) and right \(2\), so \(m = \dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{3}{2}\), not \(\dfrac{2}{3}\).
Swapped \(m\) and \(b\)! The \(y\)-intercept at \((0, -2)\) gives \(b = -2\), and the slope is \(m = \dfrac{3}{2}\), so \(y = \dfrac{3}{2}x - 2\).
The slope \(\dfrac{3}{2}\) is right, but look where the line crosses the \(y\)-axis: at \((0, -2)\) below the origin, so \(b = -2\), not \(+2\).
The line crosses the \(y\)-axis at \((0, -2)\) (so \(b = -2\)), and steps up \(3\) and right \(2\) from \((0, -2)\) to \((2, 1)\) (so \(m = \dfrac{3}{2}\)). That gives \(y = \dfrac{3}{2}x - 2\)!

questions.prompt: A student was asked to graph \(y = \dfrac{1}{3}x - 2\) and drew the red line below. What mistake did the student make?

choices.text: They plotted the wrong \(y\)-intercept — it should start at \((0, 2)\) instead of \((0, -2)\).
choices.feedback: Look at \(y = \dfrac{1}{3}x - 2\): the \(y\)-intercept really is \((0, -2)\), so their starting point was right! Check how they counted the slope from \((0, -2)\).

choices.text: They swapped rise and run — they went up \(3\) and right \(1\) (slope \(3\)) instead of up \(1\) and right \(3\) (slope \(\dfrac{1}{3}\)).
choices.feedback: For \(m = \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}}\), you move up \(1\) and right \(3\) from \((0, -2)\) to \((3, -1)\). Going up \(3\) and right \(1\) graphed \(y = 3x - 2\) instead!

choices.text: They drew a positive slope instead of a negative slope — the line should slant downward.
choices.feedback: In \(y = \dfrac{1}{3}x - 2\), the slope \(+\dfrac{1}{3}\) is positive, so the line should slant upward — just much gentler (up \(1\), right \(3\)) than the steep line they drew!

choices.text: They plotted the \(y\)-intercept on the \(x\)-axis instead of the \(y\)-axis.
choices.feedback: The point \((0, -2)\) is right on the \(y\)-axis where it belongs! The real error is the slope: they counted up \(3\), right \(1\) instead of up \(1\), right \(3\).

questions.prompt: Before drawing the line \(y = -\dfrac{3}{2}x - 1\), identify the \(y\)-intercept and one slope step. Which plan plots two accurate points?

choices.text: Plot \((0, -1)\), then move up \(3\) and right \(2\) to \((2, 2)\).
choices.feedback: Watch the sign of the slope! In \(y = -\dfrac{3}{2}x - 1\), the slope is \(m = -\dfrac{3}{2}\) (negative, not positive), so from \((0, -1)\) you move down \(3\) and right \(2\) to \((2, -4)\).

choices.text: Plot \((-1, 0)\), then move down \(3\) and right \(2\) to \((1, -3)\).
choices.feedback: Careful — \((-1, 0)\) is on the \(x\)-axis, not the \(y\)-axis! The \(y\)-intercept \(b = -1\) always starts at \((0, -1)\).

choices.text: Plot \((0, -1)\), then move down \(2\) and right \(3\) to \((3, -3)\).
choices.feedback: Swapped rise and run! In \(m = -\dfrac{3}{2} = \dfrac{-3}{2}\), rise is the numerator (\(-3\)) and run is the denominator (\(2\)), so move down \(3\) and right \(2\) to \((2, -4)\).

choices.text: Plot \((0, -1)\), then move down \(3\) and right \(2\) to \((2, -4)\).
choices.feedback: In \(y = -\dfrac{3}{2}x - 1\), the \(y\)-intercept is \(b = -1\) at \((0, -1)\), and the slope \(m = -\dfrac{3}{2} = \dfrac{-3}{2}\) steps down \(3\) and right \(2\) to \((2, -4)\).

questions.prompt: Use the \(y\)-intercept \((0, 5)\) and the dashed triangle to \((4, 4)\) in the graph below to find the line's equation \(y = mx + b\).

choices.feedback: The \(y\)-intercept is \(b = 5\) at \((0, 5)\), and the dashed triangle gives \(m = \dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{-1}{+4} = -\dfrac{1}{4}\), so the equation is \(y = -\dfrac{1}{4}x + 5\)!
You put run over rise! Always divide vertical rise by horizontal run: \(m = \dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{-1}{+4} = -\dfrac{1}{4}\), not \(-4\).
Swapped \(m\) and \(b\)! The slope \(m = -\dfrac{1}{4}\) multiplies \(x\), and the \(y\)-intercept \(b = 5\) is the constant term: \(y = -\dfrac{1}{4}x + 5\).
Watch the sign of the slope! From left to right the line slants downward, and \(\dfrac{-1}{+4} = -\dfrac{1}{4}\) is negative, not \(\dfrac{1}{4}\).

questions.prompt: To graph \(y = \dfrac{3}{2}x + 4\) inside \([-6, 6] \times [-6, 6]\), you start at the \(y\)-intercept \((0, 4)\), but going up \(3\) and right \(2\) hits \((2, 7)\) off the grid. What point inside the grid do you reach by stepping down \(3\) and left \(2\) instead?

choices.feedback: Watch rise vs. run! The vertical move (rise) is \(-3\) (giving \(y = 4 - 3 = 1\)) and the horizontal move (run) is \(-2\) (giving \(x = 0 - 2 = -2\)), so the point is \((-2, 1)\).
Because \(\dfrac{+3}{2} = \dfrac{-3}{-2}\), moving down \(3\) and left \(2\) from \((0, 4)\) lands at \((0 - 2,\; 4 - 3) = (-2, 1)\) — inside the \([-6, 6]\) grid and right on the line!
You reversed left/right, but you must reverse BOTH directions so the slope stays positive: \(\dfrac{+3}{2} = \dfrac{-3}{-2}\). Moving down \(3\) and left \(2\) from \((0, 4)\) gives \((-2, 1)\).
Careful! Moving down \(3\) and right \(2\) gives a negative slope (\(-\dfrac{3}{2}\)). To keep \(m = \dfrac{3}{2}\), reverse BOTH directions (down \(3\) and left \(2\)) to land at \((-2, 1)\).

questions.prompt: Which slope-intercept equation matches the line passing through \((-3, -1)\), \((0, -3)\), and \((3, -5)\) below?

choices.feedback: You flipped rise and run! From \((0, -3)\) to \((3, -5)\), the line moves down \(2\) and right \(3\), so \(m = \dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = -\dfrac{2}{3}\), not \(-\dfrac{3}{2}\).
The slope \(m = -\dfrac{2}{3}\) is right, but look where the line crosses the \(y\)-axis: at \((0, -3)\) below the origin, so \(b = -3\), not \(3\).

The line crosses the \(y\)-axis at \((0, -3)\) (so \(b = -3\)), and moving from \((0, -3)\) to \((3, -5)\) goes down \(2\) and right \(3\), giving \(m = \dfrac{-2}{3} = -\dfrac{2}{3}\). That yields \(y = -\dfrac{2}{3}x - 3\)!
Swapped \(m\) and \(b\)! The \(y\)-intercept at \((0, -3)\) gives \(b = -3\) and the slope is \(m = -\dfrac{2}{3}\), so the equation is \(y = -\dfrac{2}{3}x - 3\).

questions.prompt: A line passes through \((0, 3)\) and \((4, 0)\) as shown with its dashed rise-and-run triangle below. What is its equation in slope-intercept form?

choices.feedback: Swapped \(m\) and \(b\)! The slope \(m = -\dfrac{3}{4}\) multiplies \(x\), and the \(y\)-intercept \(b = 3\) is the constant term: \(y = -\dfrac{3}{4}x + 3\).
Watch the sign of the slope! From left to right the line slants downward, and \(\dfrac{-3}{+4} = -\dfrac{3}{4}\) is negative, not \(\dfrac{3}{4}\).
You put run over rise! Always divide vertical rise by horizontal run: \(m = \dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{-3}{+4} = -\dfrac{3}{4}\), not \(-\dfrac{4}{3}\).
The \(y\)-intercept is \(b = 3\) at \((0, 3)\), and the dashed triangle gives \(m = \dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{-3}{+4} = -\dfrac{3}{4}\), so the equation is \(y = -\dfrac{3}{4}x + 3\)!

questions.prompt: Starting at \((0, -4)\) to sketch \(y = -\dfrac{4}{3}x - 4\) on a \([-6, 6]\) grid, the forward slope step lands off the grid at \((3, -8)\). Rewrite the slope with both signs reversed and step backward from \((0, -4)\) — which point do you land on?

choices.feedback: Because \(\dfrac{-4}{3} = \dfrac{+4}{-3}\), moving up \(4\) and left \(3\) from \((0, -4)\) lands at \((0 - 3,\; -4 + 4) = (-3, 0)\) — inside the \([-6, 6]\) grid and right on the line!
You reversed left/right, but you must reverse BOTH directions so the slope stays negative: \(\dfrac{-4}{3} = \dfrac{+4}{-3}\). Moving up \(4\) and left \(3\) from \((0, -4)\) gives \((-3, 0)\).
Careful! Moving up \(4\) and right \(3\) gives a positive slope (\(\dfrac{4}{3}\)). To keep \(m = -\dfrac{4}{3}\), reverse BOTH directions (up \(4\) and left \(3\)) to land at \((-3, 0)\).
Watch rise vs. run! The vertical move (rise) is \(+4\) (giving \(y = -4 + 4 = 0\)) and the horizontal move (run) is \(-3\) (giving \(x = 0 - 3 = -3\)), so the point is \((-3, 0)\).

choices.feedback: The slope \(m = \dfrac{1}{2}\) is right, but look where the line crosses the \(y\)-axis: at \((0, -3)\) below the origin, so \(b = -3\), not \(3\).

The line crosses the \(y\)-axis at \((0, -3)\) (so \(b = -3\)), and moving from \((0, -3)\) to \((4, -1)\) goes up \(2\) and right \(4\), giving \(m = \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}\). That yields \(y = \dfrac{1}{2}x - 3\)!

You flipped rise and run! From \((0, -3)\) to \((4, -1)\), the line moves up \(2\) and right \(4\), so \(m = \dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), not \(2\).

choices.feedback: Reversed-order trap! The slope \(m\) is always the coefficient of \(x\) (\(4\)), and the standalone constant \(-3\) is the \(y\)-intercept \(b\) at \((0, -3)\).

questions.prompt: Inspect the \(y\)-intercept \((0, -2)\), the point \((4, -3)\), and the dashed slope triangle below. Which equation matches this line?

The \(y\)-intercept is \(b = -2\) at \((0, -2)\), and the dashed triangle gives \(m = \dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{-1}{+4} = -\dfrac{1}{4}\), so the equation is \(y = -\dfrac{1}{4}x - 2\)!

You put run over rise! Always divide vertical rise by horizontal run: \(m = \dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{-1}{+4} = -\dfrac{1}{4}\), not \(-4\).
